topics: 🐴 New Mishna: Twin Births — how many lambs go to the priest across various donkey-birth scenarios
👥 Simultaneous Twins — does Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's 'both heads at once' rule apply to donkeys too?
🐴 May One Use a Firstborn Donkey Before Redemption? — Rabbi Yehuda forbids, Rabbi Shimon permits
📜 'Your Ox... Your Flock' — two readings of the same verse yield opposite exemptions
⚰️ After the Neck Is Broken — and what counts as 'food' for ritual impurity

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Twin Births and the Limits of Benefit
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 9a–9b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After a brief coda to the Athens story, a new mishna sets out how many lambs a priest receives when one or two never-before-birthing donkeys give birth to various combinations of males and females. The Gemara first debates whose opinion the mishna follows regarding twins whose heads emerge simultaneously, then turns to a substantial dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon: may one derive benefit from a firstborn donkey before it is redeemed with a lamb? The dispute is traced to two competing readings of a single verse, and closes with the edge case of a donkey whose neck was broken instead of being redeemed.

slides.title: 🐴 New Mishna: Twin Births and the Priest's Share
slides.subtitle: How many lambs are owed, across several birth scenarios
rows: One lamb to the priest — certainly one is firstborn
Owner keeps one lamb for himself — uncertain which was born first, and the burden of proof rests on the priest
Two donkeys (first births), each bears one male
Two donkeys together bear male+female, or 2 males+1 female
One lamb to the priest — at least one male is certainly firstborn
Two donkeys together bear 2 females+1 male, or 2+2
The priest gets nothing — perhaps both firstborns were female

callout.label: The redeeming lamb:
callout.text: May be a sheep or goat, male or female, young or old, unblemished or blemished — and once the priest returns it, the same lamb may redeem donkeys again and again.

slides.title: 👥 Simultaneous Twins — Whose View Does the Mishna Follow?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yirmeya and Abaye debate the mishna's silent assumption

lines.speaker: R' Yirmeya
lines.text: The mishna's 'one lamb only' rule can't follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili — he holds it's possible for two heads to emerge in one simultaneous instant, in which case both would be firstborn.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Not necessarily. For a kosher animal, the plural verse 'the males shall be the Lord's' teaches simultaneous twins are both firstborn — but no such plural language exists for a donkey.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But a baraita has Rabbi Yosei HaGelili himself ruling that donkey-twins with simultaneous heads both go to the priest — deriving it from that very same kosher-animal verse!

lines.speaker: Conclusion
lines.text: So Abaye's distinction fails. The mishna simply follows the Rabbis, who reject Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's 'simultaneous birth' premise entirely.

slides.title: 🐴 May One Use a Firstborn Donkey Before Redemption?
slides.subtitle: Ulla explains the reasoning behind each side

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Yehuda: forbidden — no item the Torah insists be redeemed specifically with a lamb (even below its own value) remains usable beforehand
2️⃣ Rabbi Shimon: permitted — no item whose redemption medium (the lamb) is fully permitted should have its own use forbidden beforehand
3️⃣ Challenge to Rabbi Shimon: what about Sabbatical-year produce? Its redemption money is usable, yet the produce itself becomes forbidden!
4️⃣ Resolved: no real counterexample — that redemption money is also eventually forbidden, following the produce through a whole chain of exchanges — 'the last item is always forbidden'

slides.title: 📜 'Your Ox... Your Flock' — Two Readings, One Verse
slides.subtitle: Deuteronomy 15:19 excludes different firstborns for each sage

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehuda
items: 'Your ox' excludes a woman's firstborn son — labor with him is always permitted
'Your flock' excludes an animal owned in partnership with a gentile — since he holds such partnerships ARE obligated in firstborn status
A firstborn donkey remains forbidden for benefit before redemption

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon
items: 'Your ox' also excludes a woman's firstborn son
'Your flock' excludes a firstborn donkey instead — since he holds gentile partnerships are already exempt from firstborn status, no special verse was needed there
A firstborn donkey is fully permitted for benefit before redemption

slides.title: ⚰️ After the Neck Is Broken — and What Counts as 'Food'
slides.subtitle: Even Rabbi Shimon draws a line

nodes.content: ❓ Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from a live, unredeemed firstborn donkey — but what about one whose neck was broken instead of redeemed?
📖 Rabba: forbidden — a shared phrase, 'breaking the neck,' links it to the heifer of the unsolved murder (עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה), whose carcass is also forbidden

columns.label: General rule
columns.content: Forbidden-benefit items (orla, a stoned ox, this donkey) still count as 'food' for ritual impurity, since they were once fit to eat

columns.label: Rabbi Shimon's view
columns.content: None of them count as 'food' at all — 'food' (הָאֹכֶל אֲשֶׁר יֵאָכֵל) means only something you could feed to others

nodes.content: ✅ Even Rabbi Shimon concedes: meat cooked in milk IS susceptible to food-impurity, since both ingredients were briefly permitted food before being forbidden together

summary.principle: A firstborn donkey's redemption obligation is tracked precisely through every twin-birth scenario, while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon dispute — from a single verse read two ways — whether one may derive benefit from it before it is redeemed.

flowSteps.content: 🐴 New mishna: from one to two lambs owed to the priest, depending on how many donkeys and which sexes were born
👥 Mishna follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view that simultaneous twin heads both count as firstborn

columns.content: 🐴 R' Yehuda forbids benefit before redemption; R' Shimon permits it — traced to 'your ox...your flock'
⚰️ Even R' Shimon forbids benefit once the donkey's neck is broken instead of redeemed

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a firstborn donkey's status — its redemption count, its permitted use, and its impurity susceptibility — is governed at every stage by precise textual derivation

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, if a donkey that never gave birth before bears a male and a female and it's unclear which came first, what happens?
o: Two lambs go to the priest
The owner designates one lamb for himself, since the priest cannot prove which twin was firstborn
No lamb is designated at all
The priest automatically receives the male
quiz.e: Since it is uncertain which twin was born first, and the burden of proof for a monetary claim rests on the claimant (the priest), the owner keeps the designated lamb for himself.

quiz.q: How does Abaye try to explain why the mishna's 'one lamb for twins' rule doesn't contradict Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, and why does the Gemara reject this?
o: Abaye says donkeys never have twins; rejected as factually false
Abaye says the plural verse 'the males shall be the Lord's' applies only to kosher animals, not donkeys; rejected because a baraita shows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili applies that same verse to donkeys too
Abaye says Rabbi Yosei HaGelili changed his mind; rejected as unsupported
The Gemara accepts Abaye's answer without objection
quiz.e: A baraita explicitly has Rabbi Yosei HaGelili ruling that simultaneous donkey-twins both go to the priest, deriving it from the same verse Abaye claimed was limited to kosher animals — refuting his distinction.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehuda, why is it forbidden to derive benefit from a firstborn donkey before it is redeemed?
o: Because donkeys are inherently impure
Because no item the Torah insists must be redeemed specifically with a lamb remains permitted for use beforehand
Because the priest owns the donkey outright
Because the Torah never permits donkeys to be used for labor
quiz.e: Ulla explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: an item the Torah particularly requires be redeemed with a lamb (even below its full value) is not permitted for benefit before that redemption occurs.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon's reading of 'your flock' in Deuteronomy 15:19, which firstborn animal is excluded from the prohibition on shearing and labor?
o: A woman's firstborn son
A firstborn donkey
An animal owned in partnership with a gentile
A firstborn kosher animal offered on the altar
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon reads 'your flock' as excluding a firstborn donkey, since he holds that a gentile-partnership animal is already exempt from firstborn status and needs no special verse.

quiz.q: According to Rabba, why does even Rabbi Shimon forbid deriving benefit from a firstborn donkey whose neck was broken (rather than redeemed)?
o: Because a broken neck always renders meat forbidden
Because a verbal analogy links its 'breaking the neck' to that of the eglah arufah, the heifer of the unsolved murder, whose carcass is also forbidden
Because Rabbi Shimon reverses his opinion at this point
Because the priest must approve any use of the carcass
quiz.e: Rabba derives via a shared phrase ('breaking the neck') that the same prohibition on deriving benefit that applies to the eglah arufah's carcass applies to an unredeemed, neck-broken firstborn donkey.
